title: Forced Oscillations and Resonance
lead: An oscillator can be made to move by a force that is applied over and over again, at whatever frequency the driver chooses. This section shows that a system driven this way responds best when the driving frequency matches the frequency it would oscillate at on its own, which is called resonance, and that the less damping the system has the greater and the narrower that response is.
objectives: Observe resonance of a paddle ball on a string.
Observe amplitude of a damped harmonic oscillator.
summary_html:
• A system’s natural frequency is the frequency at which the system will oscillate if not affected by driving or damping forces.
  • A periodic force driving a harmonic oscillator at its natural frequency produces resonance. The system is said to resonate.
  • The less damping a system has, the higher the amplitude of the forced oscillations near resonance. The more damping a system has, the broader response it has to varying driving frequencies.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 16.24) The paddle ball on its rubber band moves in response to the finger supporting it. If the finger moves with the natural frequency f₀ of the ball on the rubber band, then a resonance is achieved, and the amplitude of the ball’s oscillations increases dramatically. At higher and lower driving frequencies, energy is transferred to the ball less efficiently, and it responds with lower-amplitude oscillations. (Figure 16.25) Amplitude of a harmonic oscillator as a function of the frequency of the driving force. The curves represent the same oscillator with the same natural frequency but with different amounts of damping. Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, and the greatest response is for the least amount of damping. The narrowest response is also for the least damping.

exercises.prompt: A famous magic trick involves a performer singing a note toward a crystal glass until the glass shatters. Explain why the trick works in terms of resonance and natural frequency.

answer.solution: The performer must be singing a note that corresponds to the natural frequency of the glass. As the sound wave is directed at the glass, the glass responds by resonating at the same frequency as the sound wave. With enough energy introduced into the system, the glass begins to vibrate and eventually shatters.

exercises.prompt: How is constant amplitude sustained in forced oscillations?

answer.solution: The driving force puts energy into the oscillator every cycle, and the damping force removes energy every cycle. While the amplitude is small the damping removes less than the driver supplies, so the amplitude grows. The energy a damper removes in a cycle grows with the amplitude, so the amplitude climbs only until the energy taken out each cycle equals the energy put in. From then on the store of energy in the oscillator does not change and the amplitude stays constant. Remove the driving force and the damping alone is left, and the oscillation dies away.

exercises.prompt: Why are soldiers in general ordered to “route step” (walk out of step) across a bridge?

answer.solution: Soldiers marching in step strike the bridge at one steady frequency, which is a periodic driving force. If that cadence happens to equal a natural frequency of the bridge, the bridge resonates: each step adds energy to an oscillation that is already there, and because a bridge has little damping the amplitude can grow until the structure is damaged. Walking out of step spreads the footfalls over many frequencies, so no one frequency drives the bridge and the oscillation never builds.

exercises.prompt: How much energy must the shock absorbers of a 1200-kg car dissipate in order to damp a bounce that initially has a velocity of 0.800 m/s at the equilibrium position? Assume the car returns to its original vertical position.

answer.hint: At the equilibrium position the whole store of energy is kinetic. How much is $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$?

exercises.prompt: (a) How much will a spring that has a force constant of 40.0 N/m be stretched by an object with a mass of 0.500 kg when hung motionless from the spring? (b) Calculate the decrease in gravitational potential energy of the 0.500-kg object when it descends this distance. (c) Part of this gravitational energy goes into the spring. Calculate the energy stored in the spring by this stretch, and compare it with the gravitational potential energy. Explain where the rest of the energy might go.

parts.hint: Hanging motionless, the spring’s restoring force balances the weight, so $\kk\kx = m\kg$.
The change in gravitational potential energy is $-m\kg h$, with $h$ the distance found in part (a).
The energy stored in the spring is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kx^2$. Compare it with the answer to part (b).

answer.solution: (a) $0.123\ \text{m}$ (b) $-0.600\ \text{J}$ (c) $0.300\ \text{J}$. The rest of the energy may go into heat caused by friction and other damping forces.

exercises.prompt: Engineering Application: A suspension bridge oscillates with an effective force constant of $1.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{N/m}$. (a) How much energy is needed to make it oscillate with an amplitude of 0.100 m? (b) If soldiers march across the bridge with a cadence equal to the bridge’s natural frequency and impart $1.00 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$ of energy each second, how long does it take for the bridge’s oscillations to go from 0.100 m to 0.500 m amplitude?

parts.hint: The energy of an oscillation of amplitude $\kX$ is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$.
Find the store of energy at each amplitude, take the difference, and divide by the energy supplied each second.
